locations.name: Tallowmere
locations.description: Major walled port on the northwestern shore of the central inland sea, built around a sheltered natural harbor where a navigable river reaches the sea. Governed locally by House Denvor under a hereditary charter confirmed by House Kharadorn.

locations.name: Millhaven
locations.description: Grain village and mill center on the River Vale, about 9 miles northwest of Tallowmere. Principal grain collection point supplying the city.

locations.name: Brackenholt
locations.description: Woodland and charcoal settlement west of Tallowmere within the Brackenwood, serving timber, charcoal, and managed woodland trades.

locations.name: Stonehollow
locations.description: Quarry settlement southwest of Tallowmere in the Greyback Ridges, supplying worked stone and quarry labor.

locations.name: Ashcombe Manor
locations.description: Agricultural estate on Ashcombe Rise overlooking the Northfields and northern road.

locations.name: Fordmere
locations.description: Upriver settlement at a dependable crossing of the River Vale, with a chartered crossing administered by House Merewick and a ferry supplement.

locations.name: Saltwick
locations.description: Working shore settlement southeast of Tallowmere with fishing, salt-working, and a modest beacon.

locations.name: Harthbridge
locations.description: Town on the South Road, about 27 miles from Tallowmere, governed under House Velleran's town charter and outside direct Denvor administration.

houses.name: House Calderan
houses.description: The ruling dynasty and Crown. Its post-Rebellion authority is substantial but constrained by the political settlement and Imperial Council.

houses.name: House Vaelorian
houses.description: Elven Great House of the western highlands. Maintains financial dominance and trade access through diplomacy and leverage.

houses.name: House Kharadorn
houses.description: Dwarven Great House and empire. Seeks independence, control of the inland sea and Dragonstone, and freedom from surface interference in clan affairs.

houses.name: House Edarth
houses.description: Human Great House of the western heartlands. Values traditional noble rights, military and agricultural strength, and resistance to excessive royal centralization.

houses.name: House Veyr
houses.description: Human Great House of the northern marches. Focused on frontier security, resources for the Northern Watch, and preserving control of the north.

houses.name: House Merrowen
houses.description: Human Great House of the eastern coast. Protects eastern ports and shipping, commercial independence, and maritime influence.

houses.name: House Denvor
houses.description: Established minor human house ruling Tallowmere from Greywatch under a hereditary charter confirmed by House Kharadorn. Locally powerful but not a Great House.
houses.heraldry_description: A black heron standing in shallow silver water upon a deep green field.

npcs.description: Intelligent, educated, patient, politically cautious, and increasingly frustrated by the limits placed on the Crown.

npcs.name: Lord Theren Vaelorian
npcs.description: Cultured, patient, calculating, and difficult to surprise. Prefers financial and diplomatic leverage to direct threats.

npcs.name: High King Durnak Kharadorn
npcs.description: Stern, disciplined, traditional, and deeply conscious of his family history.

npcs.name: Lord Garrick Edarth
npcs.description: Traditional martial lord who values discipline, loyalty, and reputation.

npcs.name: Lord Edran Veyr
npcs.description: Practical and reserved, accustomed to difficult decisions with limited resources.

npcs.name: Lady Maris Merrowen
npcs.description: Accomplished political operator with extensive commercial and diplomatic relationships.

npcs.name: Lord Oswin Denvor
npcs.description: Measured and observant, preferring negotiated solutions and predictable obligations.

npcs.name: Lady Catrin Denvor
npcs.description: Politically capable Denvor household member who maintains civic and charitable relationships.

npcs.name: Ser Edwyn Denvor
npcs.description: Recognized heir who favors greater investment in defenses and infrastructure.

npcs.name: Lady Anwen Denvor
npcs.description: Perceptive and socially skilled, with genuine relationships outside the nobility.

npcs.name: Reeve Marrec Holt
npcs.description: Methodical and protective of administrative records; values dependable civic routines.

npcs.name: Harbor Master Ysella Vane
npcs.description: Direct, experienced, and difficult to intimidate. Wants safe traffic and fair quay allocation.

npcs.name: Chief Magistrate Odran Pell
npcs.description: Patient, observant, and exacting about testimony.

npcs.name: Captain Brinna Salk
npcs.description: Practical and blunt, with strong responsibility toward her patrols.

npcs.name: Castellan Hadrik Voss
npcs.description: Veteran professional who values preparation, stores, and clear command.

npcs.name: Meret Sorn
npcs.description: Polished and cautious. Values predictable trade, secure cargo, fire prevention, and reliable records.

npcs.name: Dagna Coppervein
npcs.description: Exacting craftswoman who protects apprentices, skilled labor, quality standards, and timber supply.

npcs.name: Pellan Reed
npcs.description: Sociable, sharp, and politically perceptive. Wants fair river tolls and safe landings.

npcs.name: Tavren Selwick
npcs.description: Prosperous merchant known for paying obligations and keeping accurate cargo accounts.

npcs.name: Nix-of-the-Cistern
npcs.description: Patient and attentive to practical needs. A local contact, not a representative of all ratfolk.

npcs.name: Tikka Vell
npcs.description: Resourceful and commercially ambitious. Wants ratfolk workshops to sell openly in the Market Ward.

npcs.name: Serren Coil
npcs.description: Quiet and observant, protective of route knowledge and family shelters.

npcs.name: Miraq Ashwhisk
npcs.description: Capable independent craftswoman with a respected surface business.

npcs.name: Sister Alwen
npcs.description: Calm, stubborn, and practical. Wants food, shelter, care, burial assistance, and support for abandoned children.

npcs.name: Brother Caldus
npcs.description: Thoughtful listener who records names of the missing and lost and values maritime rites.

factions.name: Harbor Fellowship
factions.description: Shipowners and maritime interests concerned with berth access, harbor operations, and commercial predictability.

factions.name: Warehouse Guild
factions.description: Recognized warehouse operators and factors concerned with secure cargo, records, fire prevention, and access.

factions.name: Market Guild
factions.description: Established market members and merchants concerned with stalls, commercial access, and trade privileges.

factions.name: River Carters' and Bargemen's Company
factions.description: River operators seeking fair tolls, safe landings, and recognition for inland transport.

factions.name: Shipwrights' Brotherhood
factions.description: Skilled shipwright organization protecting apprentices, craft standards, labor, and timber supply.

factions.name: Ratfolk Underways Community
factions.description: Decentralized ratfolk community beneath Tallowmere with families, workshops, routes, and limited coordination. It is not a unified criminal faction or single political bloc.

quests.name: Roadside Troll Attack
quests.summary: A Selwick & Company wagon carrying ordinary commercial cargo is attacked by a troll on the PCs' approach to Tallowmere. Protecting the crew or recovering the consignment can earn a modest reward and a written introduction to Meret Sorn.

quests.name: Warehouse Guild Introduction
quests.summary: A signed recommendation from Tavren Selwick can provide the PCs a first commercial meeting with Meret Sorn. It grants credibility, not guild membership or universal trust.

regional_features.name: River Vale
regional_features.description: Principal inland route serving Tallowmere, descending from the western uplands through the farm country and into the harbor.

regional_features.name: Brackenwood
regional_features.description: Worked woodland west of Tallowmere supplying fuel, poles, timber, game, and gathered plants.

regional_features.name: Greyback Ridges
regional_features.description: Stony hills southwest of Tallowmere, with Stonehollow quarries on accessible eastern faces.

regional_features.name: Northfields
regional_features.description: Open agricultural country north and northeast of Tallowmere with farms, orchards, pasture, hedgerows, and drainage hollows.

regional_features.name: Eastern Shore
regional_features.description: Irregular shore southeast of Tallowmere with low bluffs, coves, beaches, fishing landings, and salt-working places.

regional_features.name: Old Stone Bridge
regional_features.description: Principal permanent river crossing within Tallowmere.

regional_features.name: Bellwater Pool
regional_features.description: Deep, slow pool on the River Vale upstream of Millhaven, used by bargemen as a waiting and turning place.

regional_features.name: Saltwick Beacon
regional_features.description: Modest shore beacon maintained by Saltwick boat-owning households as a navigation and storm-warning aid.

districts.name: Greywatch Rise
districts.description: Elevated heart of noble authority containing House Denvor's fortified residence, principal garrison buildings, formal gardens, and senior household residences.

districts.name: The High Ward
districts.description: Older, wealthier residential quarter with townhouses, legal offices, established temples, private courtyards, and prosperous families.

districts.name: The Old Quays
districts.description: Old working waterfront with stone warehouses, chandlers, shipwrights, rope-makers, taverns, and established shipping offices.

districts.name: The New Quays
districts.description: Expanded wharves and storage yards serving larger vessels, bulk cargo, bonded warehouses, and newer merchant concerns.

districts.name: Market Ward
districts.description: Commercial center with principal market square, guildhalls, moneychangers, inns, public notices, and specialist shops.

districts.name: Rivergate
districts.description: River-facing district of bargemen, millers, fishmongers, carters, small foundries, tanners, and laborers.

districts.name: Lantern Ward
districts.description: District of shrines, temples, charitable houses, healers, burial grounds, and religious hostels.

districts.name: The Underways
districts.description: Umbrella surface term for accessible subterranean spaces and routes beneath Tallowmere where ratfolk communities live and work. Not one unified settlement or faction.

routes.name: North Road
routes.description: Route from Tallowmere's North Gate through outer farms toward Ashcombe Manor and the Northfields.

routes.name: River Vale Road
routes.description: Western route following the River Vale through Millhaven toward Fordmere.

routes.name: Western Track
routes.description: Rough branch toward Brackenholt and managed woodland, most reliable in dry conditions.

routes.name: Quarry Road
routes.description: Southwestern branch built for stone carts climbing toward Stonehollow and the Greyback Ridges.

routes.name: Eastern Shore Road
routes.description: Coastal route southeast to Saltwick and smaller shore landings.

routes.name: King's Road / South Road
routes.description: Southern route from Tallowmere toward Harthbridge and the fragmented southern jurisdictions.

# GM Campaign Bible — Master Reference

**Visibility:** GM-ONLY  
**Snapshot:** 1 Harvestfall, 243 AC  
**Ruleset:** Pathfinder First Edition  
**Status:** Consolidated GM reference; dedicated source records remain authoritative for detailed mechanics and canon.  
**Last consolidated:** 9 November 2026

> This is the working GM-facing guide to the campaign's current world. It consolidates the setting's operating assumptions and points to the detailed records. It does not replace those records. When a detail conflicts, apply the canon hierarchy below.

## 1. Canon control and how to use this bible

### Canon hierarchy

1. Explicit GM decisions in conversation.
2. Latest approved stage, decision log, and current GM-approved change.
3. Latest dedicated lore or rules reference for the subject.
4. `campaign/Current_World_State.md`.
5. This consolidated guide and the older imported `Campaign_Bible.md`.
6. Unapproved proposals and brainstorming.

A later approved decision supersedes an earlier statement. The imported 40-page `Campaign_Bible.md` contains legacy wording and unresolved-topic lists that have since been superseded. It is preserved source material, not the sole authority. Do not reintroduce discarded names, old descriptions, or old claims that the setting is unrelated to Westeros.

### Status labels

- **ESTABLISHED:** Approved campaign fact.
- **APPROVED FRAMEWORK:** Direction and operating structure accepted; some details remain open.
- **PROVISIONAL:** Prepared for possible use, but not locked.
- **UNRESOLVED:** Do not fill in without evidence or a GM decision.
- **GM-ONLY:** Not player-facing unless deliberately revealed.

### Knowledge levels and player access

Campaign information should be separated by how a person could reasonably know it, not simply by whether the GM has written it down.

- **Common knowledge:** Widely repeated public facts, such as the names of the Great Houses, the current monarch, major cities, principal fortresses, and major geographic features.
- **Educated knowledge:** Information more readily available to literate or formally instructed people, such as dynastic history, legal precedent, distant political arrangements, and scholarly accounts.
- **Local knowledge:** Details learned by living, working, traveling, trading, worshipping, or maintaining relationships in a particular place. A newcomer may know the major town and fortress names without knowing every village, estate, road, or local dispute.
- **Specialist knowledge:** Information tied to a trade, office, faith, military role, scholarly field, or magical practice. A shipmaster may understand tides and harbor records; a scribe may understand charters; neither automatically knows the other's expertise.
- **Rumor and belief:** Claims that circulate but may be false, incomplete, distorted, or self-serving. Record the source and reliability separately from objective truth.
- **GM-only truth:** Facts deliberately concealed from the public or most characters. Do not allow them to leak merely because they appear in a campaign file.

The player-facing baseline is that all major settlements and fortresses are widely known, but not every minor settlement, private holding, or local route. Character background, upbringing, occupation, education, travel, and personal relationships determine more specific knowledge. Ancestry alone does not grant complete cultural or geographic expertise.

Do not require a skill check for ordinary facts a character would plainly know. Use relevant knowledge skills or a clear background justification for specialist or obscure information. The player handout is a filtered derivative of approved public knowledge, not an authority for GM-only truth.

### Campaign premise

The setting is an original fantasy world built around the political and dynastic framework of Westeros / *Game of Thrones*, using Pathfinder First Edition for its rules, gods, ancestries, classes, monsters, spells, and equipment. It is not Golarion and is not a direct copy of Westeros. Tallowmere is the campaign's starting city, not the entire setting. The campaign is intended to support noble politics, feudal obligations, personal ambitions, exploration, trade, and military conflict in a responsive world whose changes and consequences are adjudicated through GM judgment rather than automated simulation.

The central tone is grounded high-medieval fantasy. Supernatural horror and dangerous wilderness exist, but they support rather than replace the political and social campaign.

## 2. Current campaign state

- **Date:** 1 Harvestfall, 243 AC.
- **Starting location:** Tallowmere, on the northwestern shore of the central inland sea.
- **Campaign focus:** The setting is being developed independently of the player characters. The first region is prepared, but the wider world is not built around assumed PC choices.
- **Player concepts:** The players are revising their character concepts. Do not assume the previous vampire/ratfolk pairing, ancestries, classes, levels, relationships, private histories, or personal ambitions are current until the players confirm their final concepts and supply authoritative sheets and backstories.
- **Opening structure:** A roadside encounter involving a troll and a Selwick & Company wagon has been prepared as a possible opening. Its route, location, composition, reward, and encounter balance remain subject to the final party and GM approval.
- **Companion:** A companion concept has been discussed, but identity, statistics, equipment, role, and approval remain undecided.
- **Historical opening snapshot:** WTR-001 is retained as a dated zero-time reference on 1 Harvestfall, 243 AC. It is not a recurring simulation procedure.

### Player-character preparation boundary

Earlier player-character concepts, personal secrets, family incidents, and related hooks remain preserved in the GM-only `player_characters/` records and any linked supporting files. Treat those materials as provisional legacy concepts, not current campaign facts, until the players confirm what they are keeping.

Until the concepts are locked:
- Do not build new NPCs, factions, conspiracies, political claims, or setting history around an assumed PC backstory.
- Do not expose or use old PC secrets as active campaign facts.
- Do not assign character-specific knowledge, allies, enemies, or obligations.
- Do not finalize encounter balance, treasure, companion mechanics, or personal hooks.
- Continue developing the setting, its institutions, cultures, geography, and ordinary people independently.

When the final character sheets and backstories arrive, reconcile them against the preserved material. Keep what the players confirm, revise what they change, and leave the rest archived rather than forcing the characters into old plans.

## 3. World foundations

### Technology and everyday life

The technological baseline is high medieval: fortified stone keeps, walled towns, hereditary nobility, knights, sworn retainers, household guards, levies, conventional armies, sailing vessels, horse transport, agriculture, guilds, and skilled craft production. There is no industrial or steampunk technological culture. Alchemy exists as specialized Pathfinder-based knowledge and craft; it does not imply industrialization.

Magic is real but almost absent from ordinary experience. Most commoners have never witnessed a spell being cast or knowingly encountered a genuine magic item; arcane spellcasters are exceptionally rare, and divine spellcasters are uncommon. Most recognized wizards and other arcane practitioners serve Great Houses or similarly powerful patrons. They provide arcane counsel and services while producing a limited number of magical items under patronage. There are no magical academies or standardized wizard schools: arcane knowledge is acquired through private apprenticeship, rare books and manuscripts, or difficult self-directed study. The Collegium of the Nine Lamps is a scholarly network, not a magical academy and not a formal wizard-training institution.

Magic items are exceptionally expensive and scarce in ordinary markets. Production is constrained by the small number of capable practitioners, the time and specialized knowledge involved, the difficulty of obtaining suitable materials, and the commercial and strategic interests of patrons who restrict output and access. There is no universal enchanters' guild or central licensing authority. These social and economic conditions do not add extra crafting prerequisites, mandatory ingredients, or arbitrary costs to Pathfinder First Edition rules.

The setting distinguishes **obsydian**, ordinary black onyx, from **dragonglass**, a separate material made by dragons. Both possess necromantic properties, but they are not interchangeable and have no automatic spell effect. Their specific uses and creation details remain unresolved; see `magic/Obsydian_and_Dragonglass.md`. Player-character spellcasting and crafting follow published rules unless a specific house rule is approved. See magic/Arcane_Arts_and_Wizardry.md and magic/Magic_Items_and_Enchantment.md.

### Ancestries and societies

- Humans dominate much of the continent.
- Elves possess a major political power through House Vaelorian.
- Dwarves maintain an enduring, relatively compact empire composed of independent clans united under the main branch. It has never collapsed. The main branch is said to descend from Torag himself. Dwarves primarily inhabit mountains and underground settlements; they rarely live in conventional surface stone-built settlements. Their cultural pride favors reproduction only with other dwarves, a cultural choice rather than biological incompatibility.
- Ratfolk are naturally subterranean and live in decentralized networks rather than one unified people or government. Prejudice against them is widespread across surface societies, but it is not universal. Ratfolk are not inherently criminal, evil, diseased, or hostile.
- Other Pathfinder ancestries may exist. None is automatically designated rare or uncommon by default.

### Society and ordinary life

The continent is feudal, agricultural, commercial, and socially unequal. Most people live through household labor, farming, animal care, craft, fishing, transport, service, or trade. Noble status brings rights and obligations, but wealth, office, guild privilege, religious standing, and commercial access can also create influence.

A person's life is shaped by household, land, work, family, faith, local custom, and the authority that claims jurisdiction over them. A tenant farmer, freeholder, guild apprentice, merchant factor, household servant, sailor, soldier, and noble heir do not experience the same opportunities or risks.

Literacy is valuable but not universal. People learn through households, apprenticeship, temples, noble tutors, commercial practice, military service, and specialist scholarship. Practical knowledge is not inferior to book learning: a farmer may understand soil and seasons better than a court scholar, while a merchant clerk may understand contracts and accounts better than a landed knight.

For detailed everyday patterns, see `world/Everyday_Life_and_Material_Culture.md`. Education and access to knowledge are covered in `world/Education_Literacy_and_Knowledge.md`. Tallowmere's local communication and information flow are covered in `locations/starting_city/Tallowmere_Communication_and_News.md`.

### Religion

The Pathfinder gods are real. The continent broadly recognizes the Pathfinder pantheon, but worship varies by region, culture, institution, and individual. There is no single supreme religious authority over all faiths. Major faiths maintain independent hierarchies. Clergy and divine spellcasters are not interchangeable; a priest may conduct rites, education, charity, records, or mediation without casting spells.

Religion is woven into ordinary life as well as formal worship. Household prayers, blessings before work or travel, seasonal observances, marriage and funerary rites, oaths, charity, and local shrine customs all matter. Temples may provide instruction, records, food, shelter, mediation, and care according to their resources and traditions; no temple automatically provides every service. Worshippers of the same deity may disagree sincerely, and a public event may be interpreted in different ways. Divine magic is real, but its precise mediation remains unresolved. See `religions/Faith_in_Ordinary_Life.md` for the ordinary social experience of faith.

Each established, permanent temple maintains or designates a dedicated defender, commonly called its Temple Champion or the temple's paladin. The Champion protects the temple, its clergy, worshippers under its care, sacred property, and the surrounding community when a threat falls within the deity's concerns. Clergy primarily keep the temple and serve the faithful; they may assist the Champion in exceptional danger but are not a standing fighting force. Small shrines and caretaker sites are not automatically required to maintain a resident Champion. See religions/Religion_and_Faith.md for the office, limits, and escalation process.

The Religious Establishment has a recognized and growing presence at the royal court but no automatic Imperial Council seat. The Collegium of the Nine Lamps is an independent scholarly network, not a magical academy. The exact mediation of divine magic, major institutional hierarchies, religious courts, and the legal role of religion in marriage, inheritance, coronation, and secular law remain open.

## 4. Geography and the wider world

### Continental scale and major features

The continent's approved working dimensions are approximately 1,700 miles north to south and 1,300 miles east to west at its widest point, making it smaller than Westeros. It contains a central inland sea that shapes trade, naval power, and the strategic importance of Dragonstone.

Established geographic foundations:
- A large central inland sea.
- Dragonstone, the ancestral island stronghold of the fallen dragon-riding dynasty, now held by House Kharadorn; it is connected to the mainland by a narrow natural land bridge.
- A GM-only dwarven underground route to Dragonstone. It is not known to ordinary actors and must not be inferred by player-facing map content.
- Khar-Dum, the Kharadorns' ancestral homeland in the northeastern mountains.
- Broad Great House territorial regions and the major seats listed below.
- A harsh, sparsely populated northern wilderness beyond settled territories.
- The Frozen Expanse beyond the Ancient Barrier. Its builders and original purpose are unknown; House Veyr maintains surviving portions.

**Map discipline:** Do not invent exact borders, coordinates, route alignments, travel times, or political polygons. The authoritative artwork and calibrated atlas layers govern visual placement. Regional descriptions are not surveyed geometry. Political regions should not overlap unless a specific condition such as occupation or war justifies it. General geographic regions may overlap.

### Tallowmere — the starting city

Tallowmere is a walled port of approximately 18,000 people on the northwestern shore of the central inland sea, where the navigable River Vale reaches the coast. It is a working port and regional trade hub, not a capital or a continent-scale breadbasket. Its importance comes from the meeting of river traffic, coastal shipping, inland roads, agricultural supply, and local craft and commercial networks.

The city is ruled by **House Denvor**, a respected human minor house whose hereditary lordship is defined by a charter confirmed by House Kharadorn after the Great Rebellion. Lord Oswin Denvor holds local authority under that charter. House Denvor has no automatic Imperial Council seat. Kharadorn retains strategic rights concerning the harbor and inland-sea defense, but this is oversight of specific obligations, not ordinary city government or blanket ownership of every shoreline.

The **Chartered Council** is a seven-seat advisory and negotiating body representing principal commercial, property, craft, and civic interests. It is influential because the city depends on cooperation, but it is not a sovereign legislature or criminal court. Religious institutions have no automatic seat, and ratfolk neighborhoods have no guaranteed separate seat. Ratfolk residents may petition or seek sponsorship, but this access is structurally unequal.

The principal local offices are distinct:
- **Town Reeve Marrec Holt:** civic administration, records, notices, dues, and petitions.
- **Chief Magistrate Odran Pell:** delegated civil and criminal hearings, warrants, and judicial proceedings. Odran is also Elira Pell's father and senior partner at Pell & Daughter; this dual role is established, but no formal recusal rule is.
- **Captain Brinna Salk:** commands the Watch, responsible for ordinary patrols, public order, and arrests.
- **Harbor Master Ysella Vane:** vessel registration, anchorage, cargo declarations, quay assignments, harbor safety, and fees.
- **Castellan Hadrik Voss:** Greywatch, the household guard, stores, and defensive readiness. The garrison is not the ordinary street patrol.

Tallowmere's districts have different working and social characters:
- **Greywatch Rise:** elevated noble and garrison quarter containing Greywatch, House Denvor's fortified seat.
- **High Ward:** wealthier residences, civic offices, and the Open Ledger temple of Abadar.
- **Old Quays:** older inner waterfront, maritime trades, the Tideward Shrine, and the Blue Heron inn.
- **New Quays:** expanded wharves, bulk cargo yards, and rougher working spaces, including the Crooked Oar tavern.
- **Market Ward:** Bellmarket, guildhalls, shops, moneychangers, scribes, and the Copper Ladle cooked-food stall.
- **Rivergate:** lower river-facing working quarter with bargemen, mills, carters, landings, and the Denvor Granary.
- **Lantern Ward:** religious, charitable, healing, and burial institutions, including Lantern Hospice and the House of the Dawn.
- **The Underways:** a patchwork of subterranean homes, workshops, stores, shared infrastructure, and routes beneath parts of the city. Ratfolk communities are decentralized; the Underways are not one unified settlement or political faction, and the network is not fully mapped.

Tallowmere's livelihood depends on the surrounding region. Grain moves from the Northfields through Millhaven into the city's bakeries and markets. Saltwick supplies fish; Brackenholt supplies charcoal, firewood, poles, and rough timber; Stonehollow supplies ordinary building stone. River and coastal transport connect these places to the city. The Brackenwood Charcoal Fellowship, represented by Mara Bellwood, organizes several working families around customary access, cutting limits, fair prices, and buyer contracts; it does not own the woodland or replace Denvor oversight and individual rights. The region also includes farms, estates, crossings, woodland communities, and smaller settlements. The player-facing baseline assumes that major settlements and fortresses are widely known, but not every minor settlement or private holding. Brackenholt's charcoal work, customary rights, and relationship with the managed Brackenwood and outer Deep Bracken are detailed in `locations/starting_city/Brackenholt_Woodland_Work_and_Charcoal.md`. Animal services are limited and specific: Brindle & Sons Stables operates outside the West Gate, House Denvor maintains private household and garrison stables, Ashcombe Manor undertakes occasional horse breeding for local use, and Fordmere has stables for travelers. These are not a continent-wide animal market or public veterinary system; see `world/Animal_Husbandry_and_Working_Animals.md` and the local shop inventory.

Food is shaped by those supply lines, household means, preservation, and access to fuel. The Copper Ladle, Blue Heron, and Crooked Oar serve different public customers; Three Grain Bakery and Salt & Root Provisioners meet other everyday needs. Their documented inventories are opening reference stock, not endless supplies or a single citywide cuisine. Use `world/Foodways_of_Tallowmere_and_the_Hinterland.md` for class-based meals, food preparation, preservation, and the named businesses.

Public life is distributed rather than centered on one grand square. Bellmarket, the quays, inns, taverns, shrines, temple grounds, workshops, and residential courtyards all serve as meeting places. The Copper Ladle is an inexpensive cooked-food stall; the Blue Heron is a comparatively quiet, respectable inn; the Crooked Oar is a cheap and noisy working tavern. These are different kinds of public space, not moral categories. News travels through merchants, ship crews, civic offices, temples, households, and ratfolk courier and mutual-aid networks. There is no universal postal service or single omniscient information network. Routine Chartered Council agenda notices are posted at Reeve's Hall and the principal market.

Education is uneven and there is no universal citywide school system. The Open Ledger teaches basic numeracy to a limited number of pupils. Most practical learning comes through households, workshops, negotiated apprenticeships, religious instruction, commercial work, and private tutors where a family can afford them. Pell & Daughter provides scribal and stationer services; it is not a school. Literacy and numeracy are valuable, but practical expertise is not dependent on being able to read.

The city's care and infrastructure are practical but limited. Lantern Hospice provides charitable care and temporary assistance within its means; Edda Moss is an independent midwife and practical healer; Fenna Wale supplies mundane remedies; Miraq Ashwhisk is a specialist alchemist; the House of the Dawn provides separate religious and charitable assistance. Divine healing is not automatically available. Public wells and pumps, drains, privies, the Old Cistern, and local refuse arrangements serve different districts unevenly. There is no universal sewer network, citywide refuse service, or public-health department. The Denvor Granary is a substantial storehouse for public provisioning and charter obligations, but it does not imply unlimited emergency reserves.

Household comfort is similarly uneven. Brackenholt's firewood and charcoal supply supports heating, cooking, bakeries, and workshops; charcoal and firewood serve different needs. Streets are not uniformly illuminated, and households manage clothing repair and washing according to their means. The Blue Heron offers a documented next-day laundry service, not a citywide laundry system. See `locations/starting_city/Household_Comfort_Fuel_and_Winter_Preparation.md`.

Tallowmere has a Watch, garrison, Harbor Master, Reeve, Chief Magistrate, Master of Stores, charitable institutions, and local networks that respond to danger. It does not have an established professional fire brigade, rescue flotilla, ambulance service, public emergency-management department, or citywide evacuation plan. The Watch House contains holding cells for short-term detention, not a long-term prison. The Old Cistern can be useful during fires and dry periods, but its capacity and allocation are unresolved.

At the campaign opening, **1 Harvestfall, 243 AC**, the city is not under martial law and no citywide disaster is underway. Its active pressures include the harbor allocation dispute, warehouse fire precautions after small fires and near-misses, the expected Northfield harvest, ratfolk market access, quiet discussion of the Denvor household's future, and Kharadorn's strategic review of harbor defenses and charter obligations. These are durable current issues, not mandatory quests or guaranteed escalations. The GM decides how they develop as time passes and as people act.

For the detailed city record, consult `locations/starting_city/Tallowmere_GM_Dossier.md`. The local supporting records cover public life, calendar and seasonal routines, landmarks and routes, law and justice, emergency response, medical care, water and sanitation, household life, shops, services, and individual NPCs.

### Broad regional character

These descriptions are geographic and cultural orientation, not surveyed borders or exact climate classifications.

- **Northern Wilderness and Frozen Expanse:** severe, exposed frontier country beyond the settled northern territories. The Ancient Barrier divides the known frontier from the largely unexplored Frozen Expanse. Its builders, original purpose, and any threat beyond it remain unresolved.
- **Northern Holds and Pine Marches:** cold uplands, forests, valleys, and sparse settlements associated with House Veyr. Timber, livestock, frontier service, and imported grain are important. Supply lines matter as much as military courage.
- **Western Highlands and High Peaks:** mountain and forest country associated with Vaelorian influence, mines, passes, and old estates. Elevation creates local variation; Vaelorian does not control every route through the ranges.
- **Green Valleys and Western Forests:** sheltered valleys, woodland, managed estates, and resource communities. Customary woodland and estate rights may overlap without being identical.
- **Western Heartlands, Golden Fields, and Riverlands:** productive plains and river valleys associated with Edarth's agricultural and martial strength. Grain, livestock, landed obligations, and inland roads shape the region.
- **Central Crownlands and Royal Basin:** the inland political and administrative heart of the realm. Valedorn combines royal government, courts, markets, river transport, military administration, and scholarship.
- **Central Inland Sea:** a major shipping and naval system under Kharadorn influence. Dragonstone gives the dwarven empire a dominant strategic position over the inland sea and its approaches. That influence does not amount to blanket sovereignty over every shoreline, port, or coastal holding.
- **Northeastern Mountains and Khar-Dum:** the ancestral homeland of House Kharadorn and the dwarven main branch. Surface settlements, mines, underground communities, and clan territories have distinct relationships.
- **Eastern Forests and Eastern Shore:** coastal and river country with woodland resources, ports, fishing communities, and maritime trade. Merrowen's influence is substantial but does not mean every port is directly governed by the Great House.
- **Great Delta:** branching waterways, wetlands, river traffic, fishing, and coastal trade. Channel conditions and local authority vary.
- **Southwestern Marches:** arid highlands, dry valleys, plateaus, and oases. Water access, wells, cisterns, and caravan movement are structural concerns.
- **Southern Principalities and Southern Islands:** fertile lowlands, forests, rivers, independent cities, hereditary rulers, and maritime principalities. The south is politically fragmented, not one unified kingdom.

### Regional cultural orientation

The regional cultures are not interchangeable and should not be reduced to ancestry stereotypes. The following are broad patterns drawn from the dedicated culture records, not rules that every individual follows:

- **Vaelorian:** Long family memory, continuity, education, skilled craft, old estates, and commercial influence shape much of elite and urban life. Wealth and scholarship matter, but Vaelorian society contains tensions between old lineages, commercial houses, preservation, and change.
- **Kharadorn:** Clan identity, oaths, reputation, craft, engineering, and disciplined military traditions are important. Khar-Dum is the ancestral homeland; Dragonstone is the conquered former Targaryen stronghold and political seat. Torag is especially prominent, but dwarves are not a uniform class of miners or smiths.
- **Veyr:** Distance, difficult seasons, frontier obligations, and maintenance of the Ancient Barrier shape household priorities and public reputation. Practical knowledge, stores, service, and mutual reliance matter, while northern families may disagree with Veyr leadership over how those obligations are met.
- **Edarth:** Landholding, harvests, estate obligations, military service, and customary rights shape the Western Heartlands. Rural life is not uniformly prosperous or obedient; disputes over rents, labor, grazing, woodland, and service are ordinary sources of tension.
- **Merrowen:** Maritime trade connects shipowners, merchants, pilots, fishers, shipwrights, sailors, dockworkers, and coastal communities. Direct authority over coastal land and wider influence over shipping are related but distinct. Not every Merrowen is a sailor, and not every port is a Merrowen possession.
- **Crownlands and Valedorn:** Royal government, courts, administration, scholarship, commerce, and ceremonial life bring people and interests together. Proximity to the court creates opportunity and competition; access to office, patronage, and legal institutions remains unequal.

These patterns should guide first impressions and institutional context, not predetermine an NPC's personality, values, or loyalties. Consult the dedicated records in `cultures/` for homes, family life, food, education, religion, work, death, and internal tensions.

Use the geographic and regional records for finer detail. Do not infer political borders from these broad descriptions.

## 6. Imperial government and court

### Imperial Council

The Imperial Council has six permanent seats, one appointed by each Great House. The monarch presides but has no seventh Great House vote. It is an aristocratic negotiating institution, not a modern parliament. Council representatives are not automatically the rulers of their houses.

Current representatives:
- Calderan: Lord Chancellor Othmar Rusk.
- Vaelorian: Lady Ilyra Vaelorian.
- Kharadorn: Thane Brokk Ironvein.
- Edarth: Lady Ysabet Edarth.
- Veyr: Ser Merek Veyr.
- Merrowen: Lady Cassia Merrowen.

### Crown officers and court networks

The current Crown officers are distinct offices with different sources of influence:

- **Lord Chancellor Othmar Rusk — Royal Chancellor:** Coordinates royal administration, decrees, correspondence, government business, and the Crown's formal dealings with the Imperial Council. He also holds the Calderan Council seat, which gives him unusual access but leads other representatives to question when he speaks as negotiator and when he speaks as the king's agent.
- **Lady Meredyth Sorn — Master of Coin:** Oversees royal revenue, taxation, debts, the treasury, and financial reporting. She comes from a wealthy minor Crown-vassal family, not House Vaelorian. She believes the Crown is dangerously dependent on short-term borrowing and privileges granted to powerful houses.
- **Lord Bastian Wycliffe — Master of Laws:** A learned jurist responsible for royal justice, major legal disputes, interpretation of Crown law, and advice on the boundaries between royal jurisdiction and noble privilege. He is cautious about changing law by decree because he believes precedent sustains royal legitimacy.
- **Marshal Garran Holt — Master of War:** Coordinates the royal army, readiness, fortifications, military logistics, and defense planning. He understands the Crown's military limitations and does not assume the royal forces could defeat all six Great Houses acting together.
- **Mistress Nerys Vale — Royal Spymaster:** Coordinates intelligence gathering, informant networks, and assessment of threats to the Crown. Her network is compartmentalized and relies on servants, merchants, messengers, and personal intermediaries. Its size and reach remain unresolved; she does not automatically know every private house, clan, religious, merchant, or local matter.
- **Lord Perrin Ashcombe — Lord Chamberlain:** Manages the royal household, court ceremony, palace administration, schedules, staff, and access to the monarch. He is not the realm's chief strategist, but control over access gives him practical influence.

Religious advisers are not Crown officers and do not speak for every faith:
- **High Prelate Aveline Marr:** The most visible religious adviser at court; represents an influential religious movement, not all faiths.
- **Prior-General Odran Thrice-Blessed:** Represents one influential religious order, not the whole Religious Establishment.

Five overlapping court movements, not formal parties:
1. **Royal Court:** Queen Elowen Calderan; key associate Othmar Rusk. Stability, legitimacy, compromise, gradual institutional strengthening.
2. **Traditionalists:** Lord Garrick Edarth. Noble rights and resistance to excessive centralization.
3. **Royal Expansionists:** Princess Maerelle Calderan. Stronger Crown administration and military capability.
4. **Merchant Interests:** Lady Cassia Merrowen. Commercial stability, access, and influence of merchant networks.
5. **Religious Establishment:** High Prelate Aveline Marr. Institutional independence and religious influence at court.

Faction membership is fluid. A person may cooperate with one movement on one question and oppose it on another. Do not assume every member of a house shares the same faction.

### Constitutional balance in practice

The Council's approved operating framework establishes:
- Four of six representatives for an ordinary Council resolution.
- Five of six for protected settlement matters, including permanent changes to Great House hereditary privileges, extraordinary realm-wide levies, permanent expansion of military obligations, transfer of Great House territory or hereditary rights without consent or lawful forfeiture, fundamental alteration of the Council, or change to the succession settlement.
- A quorum of four representatives.
- The monarch may postpone a vote once for negotiation; a second postponement requires agreement from at least three representatives.
- The Council cannot command armies directly. Its leverage lies in political legitimacy, funding, cooperation, and the post-Rebellion settlement.
- The monarch retains authority for immediate defensive action in a direct attack. A prolonged offensive war against a recognized major power normally requires Council assent unless a demonstrable immediate threat makes delay unreasonable.

The Crown's officers serve the monarch rather than representing the Great Houses. The monarch appoints them where law permits, but powerful houses and court factions seek influence over appointments. Royal authority is substantial, but the Crown cannot simply administer Great House lands, command their armies at will, or impose extraordinary levies without political consequences.

For the full framework, consult `politics/Imperial_Governance_Operating_Framework.md` and `politics/Court_and_Council.md`.

The Council is not a parliament; the Crown has real authority; the Great Houses have real leverage; none is omnipotent. ## 8. History

### Dragon-riding dynasty

A dragon-riding dynasty ruled from the Imperial Seat for approximately 400 years and possessed exactly twelve dragons at its height. Dragon-bond eligibility depended on the exclusive royal bloodline. Each rider could bond with one dragon through a telepathic connection. Maintaining eligibility required reproduction within the eligible bloodline.

The dragons were enormous flying reptilian predators with strength, flight, and fire. They were not traditional intelligent, spellcasting Pathfinder dragons.

### Great Rebellion

Approximately 200–300 years before the campaign, six Great Houses rebelled for two connected reasons: to preserve their independence against centralization and to destroy dragon-riding as the basis of the dynasty's overwhelming supremacy. The war lasted a few years. Kharadorn was the principal architect and developed specialized dragon-slaying ballistas. Most dragons were killed; surviving dragons fled after losing their riders and their fate is unknown. The ruling family was nearly exterminated and the Imperial Seat fell.

### Post-Rebellion settlement

The dwarven leader who directed the rebellion ruled for more than a century after the fall. After his death, his successor inherited authority and a succession crisis followed. The successor threatened war unless a human was placed on the Imperial Seat. The head of another original rebel Great House was installed as a compromise candidate and became the current Calderan monarch. The dwarven successor reluctantly accepted the arrangement, returned to Dragonstone, and continued ruling the clans. The dwarven empire and human monarchy maintain an uneasy peace and mutual distrust.

### Historical uncertainties

- The fallen dynasty's original name is unresolved.
- The former stronghold's final original name is unresolved; “Dragonstone” is a working label.
- Exact dates of the rebellion, the Crowning, and the postwar reigns are unresolved.
- Detailed campaign histories, individual house roles, and many named historical figures remain incomplete.
- No living claimant to the old dynasty is publicly recognized. One surviving Crown Prince is a GM-only truth; he was nine years old at the beginning of the rebellion. His personal name is intentionally not recorded, and any association with a player character remains provisional pending confirmation of the revised concepts.

Use `history/Historical_Accounts_and_Uncertainty.md` to separate public, noble, disputed, suppressed, and objective historical accounts.

### How to handle historical accounts

The public account, noble interpretation, scholarly record, suppressed testimony, and objective GM truth may differ. A person may know a version that is widely believed without knowing whether it is accurate. House histories often emphasize sacrifice, lawful inheritance, and the loyalty of ancestors; rival houses may emphasize broken oaths, self-interest, or unlawful ambition.

The GM should preserve the difference between what happened, what was recorded, what was remembered, and what is believed. The surviving Crown Prince's identity and survival remain protected. The old dynasty's original name and the final name of Dragonstone remain unresolved.


## 9. Economy, military, and law

The economy is medieval and regional: land rents, agricultural production, craft guilds, ports, river transport, tolls, charters, credit, and trade. Vaelorian finance and Kharadorn strategic maritime control are important structural influences, but neither controls all commerce. Merchant interests can shape policy through credit, supply, contracts, and access without becoming a sovereign government.

Military power is based on noble obligations, household forces, local garrisons, levies, professional soldiers, ships, fortifications, and conventional siegecraft. Exact Great House force totals and readiness are not established. Do not invent army sizes or naval tonnage. The royal military is distinct from household guards and Great House forces; its exact organization and strength remain unresolved.

Feudal law is governed by homage, land tenure, inheritance, jurisdiction, charters, customary rights, courts, and service obligations. Specific charters and local customs override broad assumptions. Use `politics/Feudal_Law_and_Landed_Obligations.md` for landholding and vassalage, and `world/Law_Justice_and_Crime.md` for ordinary justice, evidence, punishment, and enforcement.

Agricultural production, food supply, livestock, storage, and seasonal work are described in `world/Agriculture_Food_and_Seasonal_Work.md`. Everyday material life, medicine, education, literacy, and travel/communication are covered in the corresponding records under `world/`. These references supply practical context; they do not establish exact prices, yields, literacy rates, weather events, or travel times where those remain unresolved.



### Agriculture, food, and ordinary economy

The continent is primarily agricultural, feudal, maritime, and regional. Grain, livestock, dairy, wool, hides, orchard produce, timber, charcoal, stone, metalwork, and fish support households and trade. The Western Heartlands, Crownlands, and fertile southern lowlands are important food-producing regions. Veyr, Kharadorn, Merrowen, and major cities depend on reliable movement of food from productive regions.

Tallowmere is a regional port and River Vale trade hub, not a continent-scale breadbasket. Millhaven and the Northfields collect grain, flour, oats, and seasonal legumes. Nearby estates provide livestock, dairy, and orchard produce. Saltwick supplies fish; Brackenholt supplies charcoal, firewood, poles, and timber; Stonehollow supplies ordinary building stone. River and coastal shipping connect these producers to wider markets.

A poor harvest does not automatically create famine. Stores, imports, credit, alternative foods, transport, and political decisions shape the outcome. Exact crop varieties, yields, prices, tax totals, and market volumes remain selective and should be established only when relevant. See `world/Agriculture_Food_and_Seasonal_Work.md`, `economy/Continental_Economic_Network.md`,  `economy/Markets_Merchants_Guilds_and_Contracts.md` for how trade, contracts, markets, and commercial influence work, and `economy/Currency_Coinage_and_Moneychanging.md` for the campaign's currency baseline and practical money use.

### Military institutions and warfare

Military power is layered. The Crown maintains a permanent household guard and a distinct royal military force. Great Houses retain their own forces and hereditary military obligations. Local lords may maintain household guards and garrisons; towns maintain watches; vassals provide only the service required by their particular charter or custom.

Kharadorn's established strengths include heavy infantry, elite armored troops, engineers, siege specialists, clan contingents, underground fortifications, and naval forces that give the house a dominant strategic position in the Central Inland Sea. This does not imply sovereignty over every shore or adjacent coastal holding. Veyr maintains the Northern Watch and mobile Marcher Companies. Vaelorian maintains a compact professional force, skilled archers, and selected mountain garrisons. Edarth's strength rests on a network of landed houses, fortifications, and military obligations. Merrowen's power includes shipping, naval tradition, port defenses, and maritime expertise.

Readiness is not mobilization. Commercial vessels are not automatically warships. A garrison cannot be counted as a free field army without exposing its post. Exact troop totals, fleet sizes, budgets, and readiness remain unresolved. See `military/Continental_Military_Institutions_and_Operational_Doctrine.md` for institutional structure and `military/Soldier_Life_and_Military_Service.md` for recruitment, training, garrison routine, campaigning, and the lived experience of service.

### Law, justice, and authority

The legal order is a patchwork of Crown authority, Great House privileges, local lordships, charters, guild rights, customary law, clan agreements, and religious jurisdiction. Law is consequential but not uniform. A charter, local custom, or recognized privilege may define rights that a neighboring jurisdiction does not share.

Local officials and magistrates handle ordinary matters; lordship courts address estate, tenant, and local disputes; liege authority may hear vassal and charter questions; Crown courts act within royal jurisdiction; the Imperial Council handles major inter-house and constitutional matters. Religious courts generally address internal religious matters and do not automatically control secular crime.

Status and wealth affect access to justice. Available remedies may include restitution, fines, forfeiture of privileges, detention, corporal punishment, or capital punishment where local law permits. Do not assume universal trial procedures, a standard penalty schedule, or automatic noble immunity. See `politics/Feudal_Law_and_Landed_Obligations.md` and `world/Law_Justice_and_Crime.md`. Tallowmere's local application is detailed in `locations/starting_city/Law_in_Practice_and_Local_Justice.md`. Emergency response, fire, flooding, harbor accidents, and recovery capacity are covered in `locations/starting_city/Emergency_Response_and_Civic_Resilience.md`.

### Medicine, education, and knowledge

Practical medicine is provided through household care, midwives, barber-surgeons, physicians, herbalists, and religious charity. These roles are not interchangeable. Magic is not routine medical infrastructure; clergy are not automatically spellcasters, and a temple cannot be assumed to provide magical healing on demand. Tallowmere's established care network is detailed in `locations/starting_city/Medical_Care_in_Tallowmere.md`; specific endemic diseases, outbreak histories, and local practitioners elsewhere remain open unless recorded.

Literacy is valuable but not universal. Household instruction, apprenticeship, noble tutors, temple learning, commercial numeracy, military training, and specialist scholarship coexist. The Collegium of the Nine Lamps is an established independent scholarly network, not a single university. Its internal ranks, training, governing body, and geographic reach remain unresolved.

See `world/Medicine_Disease_and_Healing.md` and `locations/starting_city/Medical_Care_in_Tallowmere.md` and `locations/starting_city/Water_Waste_and_Street_Cleanliness.md` and `locations/starting_city/Household_Comfort_Fuel_and_Winter_Preparation.md`, `world/Education_Literacy_and_Knowledge.md`, and `religions/Religion_and_Faith.md`.

### Travel, communication, and information

People travel on foot, horseback, carts, wagons, caravans, rivers, coastal vessels, and inland-sea ships. Roads vary in condition and maintenance. The six major continental corridors are established, but exact courses and surveyed travel times remain subject to map calibration.

Letters, official messengers, merchants, ship crews, temples, scholars, public notices, and local conversation carry information. There is no established universal postal service, passport system, or instantaneous communication network. Rumors may travel faster than verified facts. NPCs know only what they could plausibly learn through their own contacts and circumstances.

See `world/Travel_Communication_and_Information.md` and the relevant regional geography records.

### Natural world

Tallowmere's established habitats extend from the settled Northfields, Brackenwood, River Vale, Greyback Ridges, Eastern Shore, Siltfen, and city outskirts into the less continuously worked frontier environments of the Deep Bracken, Upper Vale, Greyback Heights, and Outer Eastern Shore. The Siltfen is a defined wetland region, not simply a generic marsh. The frontier belt includes old woodland, headwaters, broken uplands, wetlands, and exposed coast. These are working and traveled landscapes, but protection, infrastructure, and reliable local knowledge diminish farther from the settled hinterland.

Brackenwood is the managed working woodland around Brackenholt, with coppice, charcoal burns, gathering areas, and customary household rights. The Deep Bracken lies beyond it: older, less-managed woodland with intermittent charcoal camps and less reliable paths. Brackenholt's regular city supply is associated with the managed woodland; outer-forest camps do not establish a guaranteed supply chain or an automatic extension of Brackenholt's customary rights. The five common animals established in the Deep Bracken are not automatically confirmed in Brackenwood.

The Tallowmere wildlife catalogue contains one established ordinary-fauna occurrence inherited from the wilderness canon: deer, boar, foxes, badgers, and wolves are common animals in the Deep Bracken. This does not establish population sizes, pack territories, or their occurrence in every other habitat. Other listed wildlife and plant species remain proposals unless separately approved or observed. The wilderness framework's possible Pathfinder threats do not establish monster populations or lairs at any specific site. Do not assign exact abundance, invent migrations, or create a monster population from a plausible habitat alone. No unique magical plant or supernatural ecology is established by the botanical catalogue.

See `creatures/Continental_Ecology_and_Biogeography.md` for the continent-wide environmental framework; `creatures/Regional_Creature_Ecology_and_Field_Guide.md` for confirmed versus candidate creature occurrences and field signs; `creatures/Tallowmere_Regional_Ecology.md`, `creatures/Regional_Wildlife_Catalogue.md`, `creatures/Tallowmere_Flora_and_Fungi.md`, and `creatures/Deep_Bracken_Common_Fauna.md` for the starting region; `creatures/River_Vale_and_Siltfen_Aquatic_Ecology.md` for the distinct working-water habitats and resource practices; and `locations/starting_city/Wilderness_Beyond_Tallowmere.md` for the frontier belt.

## 10. Running a responsive world through GM judgment

The setting exists independently of the player characters. People have duties, ambitions, fears, loyalties, families, work, and limited information. Events can continue while the PCs are elsewhere, but the GM decides what actually happens. There is no automated world simulator, required world-turn procedure, or universal schedule of consequences.

### A practical approach

When the PCs leave a place, ignore a problem, take an extended period of downtime, or change the balance of power:

1. Establish how much in-world time has actually passed.
2. Identify the people and institutions directly affected.
3. Consider what each could reasonably know, afford, attempt, and risk.
4. Consider ordinary constraints: distance, season, money, manpower, law, custom, weather, supply, and competing obligations.
5. Decide which developments are important enough to occur off-screen and which can wait until play returns to them.
6. Keep the result proportionate. Not every neglected issue becomes a crisis, and not every NPC takes decisive action.
7. Record consequential events, changed relationships, new obligations, discoveries, and unresolved questions in their appropriate subject records.

Years of downtime should be handled as a sequence of meaningful periods, not as a single automatic roll. The GM can summarize routine continuity, then focus on major changes that follow plausibly from decisions, resources, and circumstances. The passage of time does not require a catastrophe or a dramatic event.

### Established structural tensions

The following are durable political and economic conditions, not active crises or guaranteed future plots:

- Crown authority versus Great House autonomy.
- Kharadorn's dominant strategic position in the Inland Sea versus Merrowen maritime interests.
- Vaelorian financial leverage and the political price of credit.
- Veyr frontier needs and southern support.
- Edarth defense of traditional noble rights.
- Fragmented Southern Reaches and their independent interests.

Use the dedicated Great House, minor-house, economic, and political records to understand these tensions. Do not assume that any one of them is escalating at the current date.

### Useful legacy records

The former world-engine folder contains useful descriptive dossiers and opening-state material. It is now a legacy GM reference archive, not an operating system:

- `world_engine/Great_House_Actor_Dossiers.md`: established agendas, relationships, internal tensions, and constraints.
- `world_engine/Continental_Strategic_Pressure_Register.md`: structural tensions and unresolved political conditions.
- `world_engine/Continental_Minor_Houses_and_Regional_Powers.md`: minor houses and independent regional powers.
- `world_engine/Regional_Holdings_and_Jurisdictions.md`: local authority, charters, and unresolved borders.
- `world_engine/Tallowmere_Political_Actor_Dossiers.md`: local houses and institutions.
- `world_engine/Tallowmere_NPC_Information_Network.md`: plausible information channels and knowledge limits.
- `locations/starting_city/Public_Life_Neighborhoods_and_Entertainment.md`: where ordinary social contact and local news exchange occur.
- `world_engine/Tallowmere_Rumor_Truth_Register.md`: rumor truth and information boundaries.
- `world_engine/Initial_Issue_Register.md` and `world_engine/Initial_Project_Register.md`: opening-state notes; use as background, not as clocks or mandatory ongoing processes.
- `world_engine/reports/World_Turn_001_Opening_Baseline.md`: historical opening snapshot on 1 Harvestfall, 243 AC. It did not advance the campaign calendar.

The GM may consult, revise, or disregard these records as the campaign develops. A record is not an instruction to make its subject act.

## 11. Calendar and campaign timeline

The dating system is **AC: After the Crowning** and **BC: Before the Crowning**. Year 1 AC is the first full year after the Crowning that established the post-Rebellion order and current monarchy.

- Twelve months of thirty days each, followed by five Yearturn days.
- Every fourth year includes one extra leap day.
- Months: Frostwane, Thawrise, Greenwake, Bloomtide, Suncrest, Highsun, Goldleaf, Harvestfall, Emberwane, Mistfall, Duskreach, Longnight.
- Week: Firstday, Secondday, Thirdday, Fourthday, Fifthday, Sixthday, Restday.
- Seasons are variable and not fixed to month names.
- The campaign begins on **1 Harvestfall, 243 AC**.

Widely recognized observances include Winter's End (Thawrise), First Planting (Greenwake), Day of the Crown (Suncrest), Highsummer Feast (Highsun), Harvest Home (Harvestfall), Night of Remembrance (Duskreach), and Yearturn. Tallowmere also observes First Safe Passage, the Weighing of Measures, River Thanks, Names of the Drowned, and the Common Table. The continental calendar is established; exact dates for these local observances and many regional customs remain open.

## 12. Open decisions and protected unknowns

Do not fill these gaps just to make the bible look complete:
- Final original names for the fallen dynasty and Dragonstone.
- Exact dates and detailed chronology of the Great Rebellion and Crowning.
- Exact Great House borders, map coordinates, routes, and local jurisdictions where not surveyed.
- Exact army sizes, fleet strengths, royal military organization, and treasury figures.
- Detailed Council voting and enforcement precedents beyond the approved operating framework.
- Full collateral family trees and household officers.
- The full reach and staffing of Crown intelligence.
- The precise nature of the Frozen Expanse, Ancient Barrier builders, and any threat beyond it.
- Exact dates and local variations for Tallowmere's civic observances, the frequency and named day of its larger market gathering, bell patterns, and gate hours.
- Divine magic's precise mediation, the specific effects and uses of obsydian and dragonglass, religious courts, and the exact legal role of religious institutions.
- Player-character names, exact statistics, equipment, and private histories not supplied in final sheets/backstories.

# Canon Register

**PC concept boundary (2026-11-09):** Earlier player-character concepts, relationships, ambitions, family histories, and attached hooks are provisional legacy material pending player confirmation. The world and its institutions are being developed independently of the PCs.

This file tracks major setting decisions and their status. It does not replace detailed records in the Campaign Bible.

## Status definitions

- **PROPOSED:** Under consideration; not canon.
- **APPROVED:** Accepted direction; details may remain incomplete.
- **ESTABLISHED:** Confirmed setting fact.
- **REJECTED:** Considered and declined.
- **REVISED:** Previously established material deliberately changed.
- **UNRESOLVED:** An open question that must remain unanswered.

## Established / approved directions

| Topic | Status | Current record |
|---|---|---|
| Rules system | ESTABLISHED | Pathfinder First Edition |
| Setting identity | ESTABLISHED | Original world, not Golarion |
| Technology | ESTABLISHED | High-medieval. No industrial or steampunk technological culture. |
| Alchemy | ESTABLISHED | Exists within Pathfinder's framework as specialized knowledge and craft; it does not imply industrialization or advanced machinery. |
| Setting atmosphere | ESTABLISHED | Grounded high-medieval fantasy and political/dynastic conflict are central; supernatural horror exists but is not the main theme. |
| Gods | ESTABLISHED | The Pathfinder gods are real. |
| Divine magic | ESTABLISHED | Divine spellcasters are uncommon and devote themselves to a god; the precise mediation of divine power remains unresolved. |
| Temple Champions | ESTABLISHED | Each established permanent temple maintains or designates a dedicated defender, commonly called its Temple Champion or paladin. The office is distinct from ordinary clergy; small shrines and caretaker sites are not automatically staffed by a resident Champion. |
| Arcane magic | ESTABLISHED | Arcane spellcasters are exceptionally rare. Most commoners have never witnessed a spell. There are no magical academies or standardized wizard schools; practitioners learn through private apprenticeship, rare texts, or self-directed study. Most recognized wizards serve Great Houses or similarly powerful patrons. |
| Magic item industry | ESTABLISHED | Magic items are exceptionally scarce and expensive. Most recognized arcane practitioners serve powerful patrons, provide arcane services, and produce limited quantities of items. Patronage, restricted output, scarce expertise, time, materials, and strategic interests constrain the market. There is no universal enchanters' guild or central licensing authority. Pathfinder First Edition crafting rules remain unchanged; no extra mandatory ingredients, costs, or prerequisites are added. |
| Ratfolk | ESTABLISHED | Naturally subterranean and decentralized; prejudice against them is widespread across surface societies, with a few tolerant or accepting communities. They are not inherently evil, criminal, diseased, or hostile. |
| Elven great power | ESTABLISHED direction | Elves possess a major political power; one of the six Great Houses is an influential elven dynasty loosely inspired by the Lannister archetype. |
| Dwarves | ESTABLISHED | The enduring, relatively compact dwarven empire consists of several independent clans united under the main branch. Khar-Dum is the Kharadorns' ancestral homeland; Dragonstone was the fallen dragon-riding dynasty's ancestral stronghold, captured by the dwarves through conquest during the Great Rebellion. The main branch is said to descend from Torag himself. Dwarves primarily live in mountains and underground, rarely in conventional surface stone-built settlements. Cultural pride leads them to reproduce only with other dwarves. |
| Other ancestries | ESTABLISHED | Other Pathfinder ancestries may exist; none are designated rare or uncommon by default. The continent remains human-dominated. |
| Six Great Houses | ESTABLISHED | House Vaelorian (elven), House Kharadorn (dwarven), House Edarth (primarily human), House Calderan (human ruling dynasty), House Veyr (human northern dynasty), and House Merrowen (primarily human maritime dynasty). Their approved words, sigils, identities, political aims, and relationship matrix are recorded in `Campaign_Bible.md`. |
| Historical distance | ESTABLISHED | The Great Rebellion occurred approximately 200–300 years before the present campaign; the exact calendar year remains unresolved. |
| Dragon-riding dynasty and Great Rebellion | ESTABLISHED | A dragon-riding dynasty held the Imperial Seat for approximately 400 years and possessed exactly twelve dragons at its height. Six Great Houses rebelled both to preserve their independence and to eliminate dragon-riding as the source of Targaryen supremacy. The war lasted a few years; most dragons were killed, the dynasty fell, and the dwarven victors claimed Dragonstone. See `World_History.md`. |
| Post-rebellion rule | ESTABLISHED in sequence | The same dwarven leader ruled for more than a century after the fall, until his death. His successor inherited his authority, but a succession crisis followed. The successor threatened war unless a human was placed on the Imperial Seat; the head of another of the original six rebel Great Houses was installed as a compromise candidate and became the current monarch. He has a legitimate hereditary claim and substantial formal authority, though the Great Houses and court factions constrain his practical freedom. Do not describe him as a powerless puppet or assume a single controller. The dwarven successor reluctantly accepted the arrangement, returned to Dragonstone, and continued ruling the clans. The dwarven empire and human monarchy maintain an uneasy peace and mutual distrust. War would not favor the dwarves, but they are not afraid of it. House Calderan is the established ruling house. The monarch's precise relationships, constraints, and sources of influence remain unresolved; no single controller is established. |
| Dragon-bond rules | ESTABLISHED | Eligible Targaryen blood was required; each rider could bond with one dragon through a telepathic connection. Eligibility depended on reproduction within the eligible bloodline. |
| Dragons | ESTABLISHED | Enormous flying reptilian predators with strength, flight, and fire; not traditional intelligent, spellcasting Pathfinder dragons. Most died in the rebellion; surviving dragons' fate is unknown. |

Exact borders, coordinates, routes, and final names remain open. |
| Legacy identities and names | APPROVED for reworking | The historical foundations are confirmed, but inherited labels such as Targaryen, Baratheon, Dragonstone, and Imperial Seat remain working names to be replaced with original identities. |
| GM authority | ESTABLISHED | GM approves whether generated events become canon |
